analysis: Giovanni Battista Piranesi at $500-800 -- and a second at 2399 for the same money. This is the best antique-plus-named-maker combination inside the band anywhere in the sale. Piranesi's Vedute di Roma and Carceri etchings are 18th-century originals by one of the greatest printmakers who ever worked, they are properly catalogued in Hind and Focillon, and lifetime impressions still trade in the low thousands. At $500-800 either these are later Firmin-Didot restrikes, or the house has underestimated them.
problems: Establish which. Lifetime impressions show a crisp plate mark, heavy inky burr in the shadows, and period laid paper with a Roman watermark. The 19th-century Firmin-Didot and 20th-century Calcografia restrikes are printed from the same worn plates on whiter, smoother paper and are worth $150-400 -- still a fair buy at $500 but not the same object. Check margins for trimming, which is the standard fault.
patience: Low. Genuine 18th-century Piranesi etchings at under $1,000 are not a recurring opportunity at a Maine general sale, and two in one lot run is unusual.

analysis: The second Piranesi at $500-800. Two consecutive lots means you get two chances and can take whichever proves the better impression -- or both, since together they are still inside a single lot's budget.
problems: Identical checks to 2398: plate mark, burr, paper, watermark, margins. Compare the two directly at preview; differences in inking between them will themselves tell you something about whether these are lifetime or restrike.

analysis: Basilius Besler (1561-1629) at $500-600. Besler's Hortus Eystettensis of 1613 is one of the monuments of botanical illustration -- huge hand-coloured engravings of the Bishop of Eichstatt's garden. An original plate is a genuine 17th-century object, which makes this potentially the oldest work on paper in the sale and comfortably the cheapest way to own something from before 1700.
problems: Besler plates were reprinted in 1640 and 1713 from the same copperplates, and modern facsimiles are abundant. Look for a plate mark impressed into heavy laid paper, chain lines, and hand colouring that sits unevenly on the surface. Original sheets are large -- roughly 22 by 18 inches -- so a small sheet is a reproduction. Five photographs.
patience: Low to moderate. Pre-1700 works on paper in band are rare in this sale.

analysis: Kathe Kollwitz at $300-400. Kollwitz is one of the major printmakers of the twentieth century -- her etchings and lithographs of poverty, war and grief are in every print room -- and much of her output predates 1926. At $300 this is well below where a signed lifetime impression trades.
problems: Which means it is probably a posthumous impression or a photomechanical reproduction, both of which are common. Lifetime impressions are usually pencil-signed and show plate tone; the Kollwitz estate and various publishers issued later editions. Establish signature and paper. Three photographs.
patience: Moderate. Kollwitz prints appear regularly; genuine signed lifetime impressions much less so.

analysis: An 18th-century miniature portrait of Oliver Cromwell at $300-400, catalogued to the century. Genuinely antique, small, portable, and with a specific historical subject rather than an anonymous sitter -- which is what lifts it above the general run of miniatures.
problems: Cromwell portraits were copied throughout the 18th and 19th centuries from the Lely and Cooper prototypes, so this is a copy of a copy in image terms even if the object is period. Check whether it is painted on ivory, which adds the usual constraint. Bidding already at $125.
patience: Moderate. There is a miniature consignment running through Day 2 (2227, 2339, 2348, 2354, 2362), so compare them all.

analysis: 'Dignified Gent with curly black hair and sideburns, OIL ON IVORY, unsigned, oval under gilt spandrel and glass, in plain rectangular leather case. Sprung clasps.' Catalogued circa 1840, so genuinely antique, cased and complete with working clasps. And painted on ivory. Federal ESA rules do allow a narrow de minimis exemption for a small, fixed, pre-1975 ivory component, and a painted wafer is a far better candidate for it than a solid carved figure -- but the exemption needs documentation of age and origin that this lot does not supply, and state law varies on top of it. Resale is recorded as zero on that basis, consistent with lot 2342. Paperwork could restore it; nothing in the catalogue is paperwork.
problems: Elephant ivory support, undocumented, resale zero. Unsigned, so no maker premium either. Reverses my earlier BUY.

analysis: 'Circa 1820 Blue-Eyed Woman with short curly black hair, black high-waisted Grecian gown, double choker with necklace and pendant, OIL ON IVORY, unsigned, original gilt cast bronze oval frame, under glass.' Catalogued to c.1820, so comfortably antique, in its original frame. Painted on ivory. Federal ESA rules do allow a narrow de minimis exemption for a small, fixed, pre-1975 ivory component, and a painted wafer is a far better candidate for it than a solid carved figure -- but the exemption needs documentation of age and origin that this lot does not supply, and state law varies on top of it. Resale is recorded as zero on that basis, consistent with lot 2342. Paperwork could restore it; nothing in the catalogue is paperwork.
problems: Elephant ivory support, undocumented, resale zero. Unsigned. Reverses my earlier BUY IF CHEAP.

analysis: A miniature portrait of Madame de la Fayette at $400-600 with five photographs. A named historical sitter, which is more interesting than an anonymous one.
problems: No date given at all, and portraits of famous historical figures were produced as decorative Grand Tour souvenirs well into the 19th century. The identification is also unverifiable. Price it as an anonymous period miniature.

analysis: 'Copy of Jean Marc Nattier (1685-1766) Portrait of Madame Sophie, oval WATERCOLOR ON IVORY, in cast brass frame.' The catalogue is candid that it is a copy after a Nattier in the Louvre, which is the right way to describe it. Watercolour rather than oil, but the support is the same problem. Federal ESA rules do allow a narrow de minimis exemption for a small, fixed, pre-1975 ivory component, and a painted wafer is a far better candidate for it than a solid carved figure -- but the exemption needs documentation of age and origin that this lot does not supply, and state law varies on top of it. Resale is recorded as zero on that basis, consistent with lot 2342. Paperwork could restore it; nothing in the catalogue is paperwork.
problems: Elephant ivory support, undocumented, resale zero. Catalogued as a copy, so no attribution value either.

analysis: Five miniatures, and the description shows the lot is mixed: 'Actress Maud Mills after Gainsborough, signed Dumont, brass frame; PLUS Madame de Montespan ... Oval OIL ON IVORY, cast brass reticulated frame; PLUS British ENAMEL ON PORCELAIN marked "Devonshire, Miss Elizabeth Chapman"; PLUS (2) Tiny French...'. So at least one is on ivory and one is enamel on porcelain, which is unrestricted. My earlier reasoning -- five objects to sort through for the price of one -- was sound, but a lot containing ivory is a lot you cannot resell as offered.
problems: At least one ivory support, undocumented, which takes the whole lot's resale to zero even though the enamel-on-porcelain piece is unencumbered. Two photographs for five miniatures, so the rest of the group's material is unconfirmed; assume more ivory rather than less.
patience: Moderate. Grouped miniatures are the value end of a category where singles are dear.

analysis: The description quotes the document in full and it is better than the title suggested. 'US Flag Ship "Franklin" Off Cronstadt, August 29th 1867. Sir, You will be pleased to have steam ready to move tomorrow the 30th inst. at 4 AM and follow my motions. In the event of separation you will proceed to Lansund in the Gulf of Finland. Very Respectfully, Your Obdt Servt, DG Farragut, Admiral, Comd'g European Squadron. (To) Commander DB Harmony'. That is a dated fleet movement order in Russian waters, from Farragut's flagship, naming both the sender and the recipient, written during the 1867 European Squadron cruise -- the goodwill voyage that followed the Civil War and coincided with the Alaska Purchase. Content of that specificity is what separates a signature from a document. It also settles my own doubt: the catalogue says 'in secretarial hand, but typically curt phrasing, BOLDLY SIGNED', which is exactly the normal and acceptable form for a flag officer's order -- staff wrote the body, the admiral signed it. At $500-700 this is inside the band and it is the best piece of American naval documentation in the sale.
problems: 'Boldly signed' is the consignor's phrase; the five photographs should let you judge the ink and the pen pressure yourself, and an autograph signature bites into the paper in a way a facsimile does not. Farragut died in 1870 and his signature is forged. Check the folds -- a fleet order was folded and carried, so expect fold browning and possibly splits at the intersections, and look for backing or silking, which caps value. Kronstadt is spelled 'Cronstadt' in the document, which is period-correct and reassuring rather than otherwise.
patience: Low. Signed Farragut documents with real naval content are genuinely scarce, and the price here is a fraction of what content like this usually carries.

analysis: A portrait of a mid-19th-century Royal Navy officer at $500-700. Catalogued to the period, and a uniformed naval sitter is more interesting than an anonymous civilian one -- the uniform dates and ranks him.
problems: Anonymous sitter and anonymous artist, and the brief flags anonymous 19th-century portraits as a weak market. Three photographs. Check for relining and overcleaning in the face.
patience: High. Day 2 carries several Royal Navy portraits (2091, 2110) plus this one.

analysis: The description makes this a stranger and more interesting object than the title. 'Full Length Portrait of an 18th c. Royal Navy Admiral, PROBABLY MEANT TO BE NELSON, EDITING OUT THE LOSS OF AN ARM. Gouache on paper, initialed ACD and numbered 1825, BACKED BY AN ALBUMEN PHOTO OF HATFIELD HOUSE.' So it is a naive or amateur portrait of Nelson with both arms restored, and the backing is an albumen photograph -- a process not in commercial use until the 1850s. That backing dates the assembly to after c.1855 regardless of the '1825' written on it, which makes the number a copy date, an inventory mark or wishful thinking rather than the date of execution.
problems: The albumen backing is the evidence and it contradicts the 1825 number -- do not buy this as an 1825 work. 'ACD' is an unidentified set of initials. A Nelson portrait that edits out his missing arm is either a copyist working from a pre-1797 source or somebody who did not know; either way it is not a documentary likeness. Flaked gold frame.

analysis: A portrait of Royal Navy Admiral Arbuthnot at $600-800. A named sitter -- Marriot Arbuthnot commanded the North American station during the Revolutionary War -- which gives it a specific historical anchor.
problems: No date, and the identification is the whole value. Portraits of naval commanders were copied repeatedly; this may be a 19th-century copy of an 18th-century original. Four photographs.

analysis: A watercolour of a First Anglo-Dutch War naval battle featuring Admiral William Penn at $300-400. The subject is 1650s naval history and Penn is the father of Pennsylvania's founder, so there is a genuine historical hook. Cheap for a marine history subject.
problems: The battle is 17th century but the watercolour certainly is not -- expect an 18th or 19th-century historical reconstruction, which the catalogue does not date. Three photographs. Check for fading, which affects all early watercolours.

analysis: An early 19th-century portrait of a New England gentleman at $800-1,000. Catalogued to the period, and New England provenance gives it regional interest a European portrait would not have.
problems: Top of the band, only two photographs, and anonymous. Compare with 2296 (circa 1810 British gentleman at $300-500 with eight photographs) which is a third the price with four times the disclosure. Anonymous portraits are a weak market.
patience: High -- Day 2 has at least eight anonymous period portraits.

analysis: The identification is much better founded than the title suggested. The frame tag reads 'James Plumridge, Esq. Father of Susanna, who married John Dyneley Prince, 1st, 1809', and the description adds that the sitter was of Littleworth, Berkshire and was father to RN Admiral and MP James Hanway Plumridge (1787-1863). That is a named, placed, dated family with a checkable public figure in it -- a different order of evidence from the usual 'identified' tag. Better still, the canvas carries an ARTIST SUPPLY STENCIL VERSO FROM A. ROWNEY & CO. OF LONDON, which is a physical, dateable maker's mark on the support and corroborates an English early-19th-century origin independent of the tag.
problems: The condition line is real damage and I had not accounted for it: 'PUNCTURE in background upper right, REPAIRED PUNCTURE at lapel.' One unrepaired hole and one repaired one, and the repaired one is in the sitter's coat where it will always be visible under raking light. That is why a portrait with this much documentation is $300-500. Unsigned, so the painter is unknown regardless of how well the sitter is identified.

analysis: A circa-1860 portrait of a woman, probably Swiss, at $300-500 -- the cheaper of a pair with 2420 at $800-1,200. Catalogued to a decade so genuinely antique, and the cheap one of two comparable lots is usually the better buy.
problems: 'Probably Swiss' is the cataloguer guessing at origin. Anonymous sitter, weak market. Three photographs.

analysis: A mid-19th-century portrait of a woman, probably Swiss, at $800-1,200 -- the dearer companion to 2421.
problems: Only just inside the band, and no stated reason why it is triple 2421's estimate. Compare both; if the difference is size rather than quality, buy the cheap one.

analysis: An 18th-century portrait of William Penn at $600-800. Catalogued to the century, so genuinely antique, and Penn is a named historical subject with American resonance -- which matters more here than a generic period portrait.
problems: Penn portraits derive from a small number of prototypes and were copied continuously; this will be a period copy rather than a life portrait. Note 2164 offers a fabric print of Penn at the same estimate, so there is a Penn sub-theme in this consignment. Four photographs.

analysis: An early 19th-century pastel fruit still life at $800-1,200. Catalogued to the period, and still lifes are a more saleable subject than anonymous portraits.
problems: Only just inside the band. Pastel is the most fragile medium there is -- it smudges, and any moisture behind the glass is fatal. Check it has never been reglazed carelessly. Three photographs.

analysis: An early 18th-century painting of Cupid, unframed, at $600-800. Catalogued to the early 18th century, which makes it one of the oldest paintings in the sale inside the band -- and unframed means you can examine the canvas edges, tacking margins and stretcher directly, which is exactly how you confirm the date.
problems: Unframed also means framing cost. Only two photographs. Expect relining, old restoration and darkened varnish on a canvas of this age -- all normal, none disqualifying, but they cap the value.
patience: Low to moderate. Genuine early 18th-century oils under $1,000 are uncommon.

analysis: A small 19th-century Dutch genre painting at $500-700 with twelve photographs -- by far the most thoroughly documented lot in this section, which for a $500 picture is unusual and useful. Catalogued to the century. Small Dutch genre panels are competently made and easy to live with.
problems: Anonymous, and 19th-century Dutch genre was produced in enormous quantity for the export market. Twelve photographs means you can assess condition properly before bidding -- use them.

analysis: A Barbizon School landscape at $500-700, with a second at 2367 for the same money. Barbizon pictures are honest 19th-century French landscape work.
problems: Per the standing principles, 'School' with no name attached is a hopeful label rather than an attribution -- price it as the anonymous work it is. No date either. Two comparable lots means no scarcity. Six photographs each.

analysis: The second French Barbizon School landscape at $500-700.
problems: Same as 2357. Bid whichever is in better condition and let the other go.

analysis: Alfred Heaton Cooper (1864-1929) at $300-400. Cooper was a well-known Lake District watercolourist whose work still sells steadily in Britain, and he died in 1929 so most of his output predates 1926. Cheap for a named artist with a real market.
problems: That market is in England, so resale would mean consigning abroad. Watercolour, so check for fading -- Cooper's blues are particularly prone. Five photographs.

analysis: Peter Graham (Scotland, 1836-1921) at $400-600. Graham was a Royal Academician whose Highland cattle and coastal scenes were enormously popular in the Victorian period -- and whose prices have fallen a long way since. Almost all his output predates 1926.
problems: The fall in Victorian academic painting is the point: Graham canvases that made four figures a century ago now struggle. Genuinely antique and by a properly documented RA, but do not expect appreciation. Five photographs.

analysis: Georges W.B. Brown (Scotland, 1831-1909) at $300-400. Died in 1909, so unambiguously antique. A minor Scottish landscape painter.
problems: Very thin market record. Three photographs. Bought for the age and the picture, not the name.

analysis: A Victorian watercolour of a Scottish loch at $400-600. Catalogued as Victorian so genuinely antique, and anonymous so no maker premium.
problems: Highland loch watercolours were produced in vast numbers for the Victorian tourist trade. Fading is the standard problem. Three photographs.

analysis: William Gwynn of Ludlow (circa 1795-1838) at $600-800. Died in 1838, so unambiguously antique by nearly a century, and the catalogue names both artist and town -- a specific provincial English painter rather than an anonymous hand.
problems: An obscure provincial name with essentially no auction record, so the estimate rests on the picture rather than the market. Three photographs. Check for relining.
patience: Moderate. Firmly pre-1840 signed pictures inside the band are not common.

analysis: Henry Noble (UK, 1896-1984) at $300-400 with four photographs.
problems: No criteria fit -- modern, British, minor name. Cheap enough to be a decorating purchase only.

analysis: John Sutton (UK, 1935- ) at $600-800. A living British marine painter with a solid commercial following.
problems: No criteria fit: modern, British, living. His market is in the UK.

analysis: Frank Penfield (NY/France, 1849-1921) at $600-800. Died in 1921, so unambiguously antique. Five photographs.
problems: Thin market record. Not to be confused with Edward Penfield, the far better-known poster designer -- check which Penfield, because the name similarity could mislead in either direction.

analysis: Frederick Trapp Friis (1865-1909) at $700-900 with seven photographs. Died in 1909, so genuinely antique, and the multi-country attribution suggests an academically trained painter.
problems: Obscure name with little market presence. Top of the band. Note lot 1295 in Day 1 is by an artist using the alias 'Th. Friis' -- unrelated, but worth not confusing them.

analysis: Albert Jean Adolphe (PA, 1865-1940) at $700-900 with five photographs. A Philadelphia painter whose career begins well before 1926.
problems: Border on age until dated. Minor name. Top of the band.

analysis: Edward Emerson Simmons (MA/NY, 1852-1931) at $800-1,200. Simmons was one of the Ten American Painters -- a genuine Impressionist of standing, better known as a muralist -- so the name carries real weight and most of his output predates 1926.
problems: Only just inside the band. His easel paintings are less sought after than his murals are admired, and the market for the Ten varies enormously by member. Five photographs.
patience: Moderate. A member of the Ten inside the band is worth a look.

analysis: Louis Mathieu Didier Guillaume (1816-1892) at $500-700. Died in 1892, so unambiguously antique. A French-born painter who worked in Virginia and Washington and painted Confederate-era portraits.
problems: Thin market. The American Civil War-era connection is the most interesting thing about him and the catalogue does not say whether this work relates to it. Four photographs.

analysis: Louis Auguste Lapito (1803-1874) at $600-800. Died in 1874 so firmly antique, and Lapito was a Barbizon-adjacent French landscape painter -- a documented name rather than the anonymous 'Barbizon School' labels at 2357 and 2367.
problems: Minor within the Barbizon circle and the market for French 19th-century landscape is soft. Four photographs. But a named, dated, genuinely antique landscape at $600 is a fair proposition.

analysis: Guglielmo Innocenti (Italy, 1871-1961) at $600-800 with four photographs. Career begins well before 1926.
problems: Border on age. Minor Italian name with a market concentrated in Italy.

analysis: Edmund Quincy (MA/Italy, 1903-1997) at $600-800 with five photographs. A Boston-connected modernist with a modest following.
problems: Modern, no Maine link. Note the catalogue runs the state and date together as 'MA/ITALY,1903-1997' without a space -- minor, but of a piece with the sloppiness elsewhere.

analysis: Yitzhak Frenkel-Frenel at $600-800 -- the second of two in the sale, with 1050 in Day 1.
problems: No criteria fit. Israeli market.

analysis: Urbain Emmanuel Huchet (France, 1930-2014) at $400-600. A commercial French painter and lithographer.
problems: No criteria fit. Huchet's output is largely graphic and widely distributed.

analysis: Leo Laporte-Blairsy (France, 1867-1923) at $500-700. Died in 1923, so antique-eligible, and he was a genuine Art Nouveau sculptor -- his lamps and figures in the Nouveau idiom are properly of the period, which makes this a criterion-three candidate.
problems: Establish what it actually is -- Laporte-Blairsy is known for bronze and pewter figures and lamps, so this may not be a painting at all despite where the catalogue places it. Later casts exist. Three photographs.
patience: Moderate. Genuine Nouveau-period sculpture inside the band is uncommon in this sale.

analysis: A framed Royal Vienna porcelain plaque with a Napoleon painting at $800-1,200. Hand-painted porcelain plaques are a distinct collecting category and Napoleonic subjects have their own following.
problems: 'Royal Vienna' is a style designation more than a maker -- the original Vienna manufactory closed in 1864, and the overwhelming majority of 'Royal Vienna' pieces are later Bohemian and German copies bearing a spurious beehive mark. Check the mark and the quality of the painting. Five photographs.
patience: High. Royal Vienna style plaques are abundant.

analysis: A life-sized portrait of an 18th-century French bishop at $700-1,000. Catalogued to the century so genuinely antique, and an ecclesiastical portrait has a certain presence.
problems: 'Life-sized' is the practical problem -- this will be a very large canvas needing a wall and a ceiling to match, and large anonymous portraits are among the hardest pictures to resell. Expect relining and old restoration. Four photographs.
patience: High. Large anonymous period portraits routinely fail to sell.

analysis: A Neoclassical painting signed 'La Rose' at $800-1,200 with five photographs.
problems: An unidentified signature per the standing principles -- 'La Rose' resolves to no established painter, so do not pay named-maker money. No date given either. Price it as an anonymous Neoclassical picture.

analysis: Johannes Adam Simon Oertel (1823-1909) at $500-1,000. Died in 1909 so unambiguously antique, and Oertel is a documented American painter -- best known for the religious image 'Rock of Ages', which was reproduced everywhere in the 19th century.
problems: The wide $500-1,000 spread signals the house is unsure. Establish whether this is an original oil or one of the many prints after his popular compositions. Five photographs.

analysis: A 19th-century painting of a naval battle at $800-1,000. Catalogued to the century and a marine subject, so it hits the antique criterion and the marine interest together.
problems: Top of the band, anonymous. Naval battle scenes are dramatic but dark, and the varnish on 19th-century marine oils yellows badly -- what looks like night may be dirt. Four photographs.

analysis: A terracotta funerary jar with a mismatched portrait lid at $600-800. The catalogue is unusually honest in flagging the mismatch -- a canopic or funerary jar married to a lid from something else.
problems: Antiquities without provenance are a category to avoid: authenticity is hard to establish, and legal title and export documentation will not accompany a $700 lot. The acknowledged mismatch means it is already a composite object. Seven photographs, which is good disclosure for what it is.
patience: Irrelevant -- the provenance problem is decisive.

analysis: An Indo-Persian miniature visionary painting at $500-700. Indo-Persian miniatures are finely made objects with a genuine following.
problems: No date at all, and this is a category where 20th-century Indian workshop production for the tourist trade is enormous and near-indistinguishable in photographs. Only two photographs. Check the paper, the burnishing and whether the gold is applied leaf or paint.

analysis: A mid-19th-century Indian Mughal miniature at $200-300 -- one of three (2447, 2449, 2450) at the same price. Catalogued to the mid-19th century so genuinely antique, and at $200 among the cheapest antiques in the sale.
problems: Same authenticity caution as 2445 -- but at $200 the risk is proportionate. Two photographs each. Three comparable lots means you can be selective; buy the one with the best-preserved gold and the least flaking.
patience: Moderate -- three chances at essentially the same object.

analysis: The second mid-19th-century Mughal miniature at $200-300.
problems: Same as 2447.

analysis: A large mid-19th-century Mughal miniature at $200-300 -- larger than 2447 and 2449 for the same money, which makes it the value pick of the three if condition is comparable.
problems: Larger sheets flex and crack more. Same authenticity checks.

analysis: Three Chinese export pith paper paintings of figural boats and processional scenes at $600-800. Catalogued to the century, and boat subjects connect loosely to the marine theme.
problems: Pith paper is extraordinarily fragile -- it cracks and flakes and cannot be restored. Three sheets means three things to be damaged. Note Day 1 offers the same material cheaper at 1403 and 1409. Four photographs.
patience: High -- four pith lots across the sale.

analysis: Three 19th-century Hispanic Colonial pith paintings, two framed, at $600-800. Catalogued to the century. Hispanic colonial pith work is less common than the Chinese export material.
problems: Same fragility. 'Hispanic Colonial' is a loose designation covering a wide geography and date range. Four photographs.

analysis: A Chinese ancestor portrait group painting at $600-800. Ancestor portraits are a distinct and genuinely interesting category -- formal, hieratic images made for family shrines.
problems: 'Late Qing to Republic' spans roughly 1875-1949, straddling the antique line, so the house is not committing. Ancestor portraits are also widely reproduced. Three photographs.

analysis: A modern Chinese painting, framed, at $200-400. The catalogue says modern, which settles it.
problems: No criteria fit at all, and only two photographs. Modern Chinese decorative paintings are produced in enormous volume.

analysis: Peter Meindl (NH, 1899-1980) at $800-1,200 with four photographs. A New Hampshire painter, so northern New England but not Maine.
problems: Only just inside the band. Minor name with a thin record.

analysis: Wendell Thompson Perkins (MA/FL, 1927-1997) at $800-1,200 with five photographs.
problems: Only just inside the band, no criteria fit beyond a name.

analysis: Yngve Edward Soderberg (CT/IL, 1896-1971) at $600-800. Soderberg was a Mystic, Connecticut marine painter and etcher whose yachting subjects have a following among sailing collectors.
problems: Only one photograph, which is poor. Establish the medium -- his etchings are $150-300, his oils considerably more, and one photograph will not tell you.

analysis: Dolores Hackenberger (PA, 1930-2024) at $800-1,000 -- the dearest of four Hackenberger lots (2138, 2140, 2143, 2145). Recently deceased Pennsylvania folk-style painter.
problems: Four lots by one artist means no scarcity. 2145 at $400-600 is the cheapest entry. No criteria fit.

analysis: Second Dolores Hackenberger at $600-800 with five photographs.
problems: Same as 2138.

analysis: Third Dolores Hackenberger at $600-800.
problems: Same as 2138.

analysis: The cheapest Dolores Hackenberger at $400-600 -- and the last of the four, which is the position where bidder fatigue helps most.
problems: No criteria fit, but if you want one of these it is this one.

analysis: Fredrik Michael Wood (CA, 1944- ) at $2,000-3,000 -- the major work of the five-lot Wood group in the California consignment.
problems: Out of band and wrong coast. Its role is positional: a $2,000-3,000 Wood in the same sale as four at $400-600 tells you where the consignor thinks the value sits.

analysis: Emily Eveleth (CT, 1960- ) at $1,200-1,500. A contemporary painter best known for large, oddly monumental doughnut paintings, with genuine gallery and critical standing.
problems: Out of band. Living artist with an active primary market, so auction offers no discount.

analysis: Austin Merrill Mecklem (NY/WA, 1894-1951) at $1,200-1,500. A WPA-era American Scene painter with murals in public buildings; part of his output predates 1926.
problems: Out of band. Three photographs. WPA-era regionalism has a modest but real market.
